title: Dynetics, Inc. v. United States
articleTitle: A Deep Analysis of Dynetics, Inc. v. United States and the Funded Research Exclusion in R&D Tax Credits
court: United States Court of Federal Claims
subject: Funded Research Exclusion
summary: Dynetics v. United States (Fed. Cl. 2015) held that research performed by an engineering contractor under seven sample cost-reimbursement, time-and-materials, and fixed-price level-of-effort contracts was funded research excluded from the federal R&D tax credit under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), because payment was not contingent on research success and, for two contracts, Dynetics retained no substantial rights.

body.text: Executive Summary & Case Background
Procedural Posture and Nature of the Taxpayer's Claim

In Dynetics, Inc. and Subsidiaries v. United States, Docket No. 12-576T, 121 Fed. Cl. 492 (2015) (an opinion and order on cross-motions for partial summary judgment, rather than a final judgment, which resolved only the funded-research question and directed the parties to file a joint status report by June 30, 2015; the opinion itself reflects no appellate affirmance), the United States Court of Federal Claims issued a foundational ruling defining the boundaries of the "funded research" exclusion to the federal research and development (R&D) tax credit. The plaintiff, Dynetics, Inc. (together with its subsidiaries), is an engineering, scientific, and applied research corporation headquartered in Huntsville, Alabama, specializing in defense, aerospace, intelligence, and tactical weapons systems.

Dynetics filed amended federal income tax returns for three tax periods seeking multi-million-dollar tax refunds based on qualified research expenses (QREs) claimed under Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C.) § 41 for engineering and development work performed across more than 100 contracts with United States government agencies, a university, and commercial prime contractors. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) disallowed the refund claims; in the ensuing litigation, the government argued that the engineering activities under the sample contracts constituted "funded research" under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) because Dynetics would be paid regardless of whether its research succeeded and, for two sample contracts (UAH01 and NT001), because Dynetics retained no substantial rights in the research results. Dynetics timely filed a refund suit in the Court of Federal Claims on September 7, 2012. To streamline discovery and adjudication across the more than 100 disputed agreements, the parties stipulated to a representative sampling methodology, selecting seven sample contracts for resolution via cross-motions for partial summary judgment pursuant to Rule 56(a) of the Rules of the United States Court of Federal Claims (RCFC).
The Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

Within the United States federal tax system, I.R.C. § 41(a) and (b) permit taxpayers to claim an incremental credit against federal income tax for QREs—comprising in-house wages, supplies, computer leasing costs, and 65 percent of eligible contract research expenses—paid or incurred in carrying on a trade or business. To qualify as "qualified research" under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1), an activity must satisfy the statutory Four-Part Test: the expenditures must be eligible for treatment as expenses under I.R.C. § 174 (the Section 174 test); the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature (the technological information test); the application of that information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer (the business component test); and substantially all of the activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality (the process of experimentation test).

Even where a taxpayer's engineering activities satisfy the Four-Part Test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1), the statute imposes eight categorical exclusions under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4). Chief among these for government and commercial contractors is I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), which excludes from qualified research "[a]ny research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or governmental entity)". The statutory text does not independently define the term "funded," delegating the operational framework to Treasury Regulations. Specifically, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(9) directs that "[t]o determine the extent to which research is so funded, § 1.41-4A(d) applies".

Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), the determination of whether contract research is "funded" requires a holistic examination of all agreements (not merely dedicated research contracts) entered into between the researcher and the customer across a strict two-prong legal standard. The first prong, governed by Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1), evaluates financial risk and contingency of payment, stipulating that research is not treated as funded if amounts payable under the agreement are "contingent on the success of the research and thus considered to be paid for the product or result of the research" rather than for the mere performance of the research activity. This provision cross-references Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2), operating as a statutory "mirror rule" intended by Congress to allocate the tax subsidy to whichever contracting party bears the actual financial risk of technical failure. As established by the Federal Circuit in Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), a contractor bears the financial risk of failed research only when its right to receive or retain payment is contractually conditioned upon successfully developing and delivering a technically compliant product or research result accepted by the client.

The second prong of the regulatory framework, governed by Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2) and (3), evaluates the retention of substantial rights in the research outcomes. Even if a contractor bears financial risk—or where the parties must determine whether research is fully or partially funded—Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2) mandates that if a taxpayer performing research for another person "retains no substantial rights in research under the agreement providing for the research, the research is treated as fully funded for purposes of section 41(d)(4)(H), and no expenses paid or incurred by the taxpayer in performing the research are qualified research expenses". Under Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), a taxpayer retains substantial rights only if the research agreement itself preserves the taxpayer's right to use or exploit the results of the research in its trade or business without having to pay for that right—a determination made by reference to the research agreements alone—and Dynetics applied this standard to hold that a right of use dependent on the customer's authorization does not suffice. Furthermore, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2) (incorporating Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(a)(3)) explicitly states that "[i]ncidental benefits to the taxpayer from performance of the research (for example, increased experience in a field of research) do not constitute substantial rights in the research". Where a taxpayer retains substantial rights but payment is not contingent on technical success, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i) treats the research as partially funded to the extent of the payments to which the taxpayer becomes entitled, permitting a pro-rata credit only if total research expenditures exceed the customer's funding.
The Tax Authority's Challenge and the Court's Final Holding

In Dynetics, the United States argued on summary judgment that under each sample contract Dynetics would be paid regardless of whether its research succeeded, and that on two sample contracts—the UAH01 subcontract with the University of Alabama in Huntsville (performed under a NASA cooperative agreement) and Task Order 169 of the NT001 intelligence contract—Dynetics retained no substantial rights in the research results. Dynetics countered that FAR inspection clauses, commercial rejection and warranty clauses (BOE12), a contractual warranty clause supported by Alabama law (UAH01), termination clauses, the undefinitized initial form of three contracts, and general business risks—supplemented by eight witness affidavits attesting to a long-standing "course of dealing" in which Dynetics voluntarily corrected defective work and absorbed cost overruns at its own expense—placed the company at financial risk under Fairchild. Dynetics further contended that it retained substantial rights under Lockheed Martin because, on UAH01, its non-patentable technology fell outside the subcontract's intellectual property vesting clause, and, on NT001, the skills and advancements it developed could be reused, its results could be used for other agencies following government authorization, its models were severable from the intelligence material, and FAR 52.227-11 preserved its patent rights.

On May 31, 2015, Chief Judge Patricia E. Campbell-Smith granted the government's motion for partial summary judgment on the funded research question and denied Dynetics' cross-motion. Applying the presumption of correctness that attaches to the Commissioner's determinations in tax refund suits (Bubble Room, Inc. v. United States, 159 F.3d 553 (Fed. Cir. 1998); Estate of Rubinstein v. United States, 119 Fed. Cl. 658 (2015)) and the taxpayer's burden of proving by a preponderance of the evidence that the determination is incorrect and establishing entitlement to the specific refund claimed (Cook v. United States, 46 Fed. Cl. 110 (2000); Helvering v. Taylor, 293 U.S. 507 (1935)), the Court of Federal Claims held that the research performed under all seven sample contracts constituted "funded research" under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d).

The court ruled that Dynetics' cost-reimbursement, time-and-materials, and fixed-price level-of-effort contracts did not condition payment on the technical success of the research, that FAR inspection clauses lacking the rejection language and acceptance-limited payment terms present in Fairchild do not shift financial risk to the contractor, and that course-of-dealing affidavits are parol evidence that cannot vary unambiguous written contract terms—and, in any event, showed only Dynetics' unilateral practices rather than a joint understanding with its contracting partners. Additionally, for the two contracts evaluated under the second regulatory prong, the court held that Dynetics failed to retain substantial rights because the UAH01 subcontract vested all intellectual property rights in the University and the NT001 contract's DD Form 254 security requirements left Dynetics with no right to use results containing intelligence information without government authorization.

body.text: Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

The disqualification of Dynetics' R&D tax credit claim stemmed from a series of compounding legal, contractual, and evidentiary deficiencies. Rather than evaluating its government and commercial subcontracts through the strict textualist lens applied by federal courts in tax refund litigation, Dynetics relied on generalized business risks, standard procurement clauses, and post-hoc witness testimony. A granular examination of the ruling reveals five interconnected areas of legal failure.
Failure to Establish Financial Risk Across Diverse Procurement Pricing Structures

The central legal failure in Dynetics was the taxpayer's inability to demonstrate that its right to payment under the seven sample contracts—designated by project codes AF007, AMS01, AR005, BOE12, NT001, UAH01, and AR009—was contingent upon the technical success of the research as required by Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1). Throughout the litigation, Dynetics attempted to liken its agreements to the contract held to be unfunded in Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995). However, the Court of Federal Claims highlighted the stark structural divergence between the contract in Fairchild and the procurement vehicles executed by Dynetics.

In Fairchild, the U.S. Air Force contracted for the development of two prototype Next Generation Trainer (NGT) aircraft (the T-46A) under a contract incorporating more than 1,000 pages of binding technical specifications. Crucially, Fairchild expressly accepted "Total System Responsibility" for the NGT system, and the incorporated Defense Acquisition Regulation provisions permitted the Air Force to reject defective work, require Fairchild to correct it at its own expense, or accept it subject to an equitable price reduction, while payment was made only for work delivered and accepted—so that the contract explicitly placed solely on Fairchild the risk of failure of every line item. By contrast, Dynetics executed contracts governed by fundamentally different federal procurement pricing mechanisms that insulated the contractor from the financial risk of technical failure.

With respect to Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee (CPFF) contracts, specifically AF007 and NT001, the payment mechanics guaranteed cost recovery regardless of technical outcome. Under Contract AF007 (Contract No. F08630-03-C-0034), awarded by the U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory to develop and test 14 tailkits capable of carrying 21,600 pounds of ammunition for deployment at a specified target, and Contract NT001 (Contract No. MDA908-99-D-0001), issued in 1999 by the Defense Intelligence Agency's Missile & Space Intelligence Center (MSIC) for tasks associated with understanding foreign missile systems and U.S. capability to defend against them, Dynetics was compensated on a cost-reimbursement basis. Under federal procurement law, a CPFF contract obligates the government to reimburse the contractor for all allowable, allocable, and reasonable costs incurred up to the obligated funding ceiling, plus a fixed fee, regardless of whether the research produces a working prototype or successful analytical outcome. The same result applied to Subcontract UAH01, a cost-plus-fixed-fee level-of-effort subcontract issued by the University of Alabama in Huntsville under a NASA/Marshall Space Flight Center cooperative agreement, where the court held that Dynetics could not rely on Alabama warranty statutes not incorporated into the subcontract because, under Lockheed Martin, risk must be determined by reference to the research agreement itself.

A similar lack of contingency defeated Dynetics' Time-and-Materials (T&M) contract, designated as BOE12, issued by The Boeing Company, under which Dynetics assisted in developing a system to defend the United States against long-range ballistic missile attacks. Under a T&M payment mechanism, the contractor bills at fixed, fully burdened hourly labor rates for each labor category plus the actual cost of materials. Dynetics argued that the Rejection and Warranty clauses of Boeing's General Provisions (GP3) put it at risk, but the court held that reperformance "at Seller's expense" was defined as limited to Dynetics' hourly rate excluding profit, that Boeing's right to charge Dynetics for replacement services arose (after the court construed an ambiguity against Boeing as drafter) only if Dynetics failed or refused to correct or reperform—a risk not attributable to the failure of the research—and that the materials warranty was irrelevant because only wages were claimed.

The court also scrutinized Fixed-Price Level-of-Effort (FP-LOE) contracts, exemplified by Contract AR009 (Contract No. DAAH01-02-C-R170), issued by the U.S. Army Aviation & Missile Command, under which Dynetics was engaged to design, develop, and test aerodynamic vehicles, including missiles, aviation systems, and targets. Dynetics contended that AR009 was a "hybrid" contract because it required specified deliverables (such as the twenty hardware items listed in Technical Directive Order 8) and allowed Dynetics to vary hours by plus or minus 10 percent, and it relied on the fixed-price inspection clause (FAR 52.246-7) to argue that it carried financial risk. The court pierced the "fixed-price" label, explaining that under FAR 16.207-2 payment in an FFP-LOE contract is based on the effort expended rather than on the results achieved, that FAR Part 35 contemplates FFP-LOE contracts for development work including prototyping and engineering testing, and that the labor-mix flexibility showed only discretion in how Dynetics provided the purchased level of effort. Once Dynetics delivered the contracted level of effort, the government was legally obligated to pay the contract price regardless of whether the aerodynamic designs succeeded or failed.

Dynetics' arguments on Contracts AR005 and AMS01 likewise failed the Fairchild standard. Contract AR005 (Contract No. DAAH01-02-C-0080), issued by the U.S. Army Aviation & Missile Command for work including calibration shelters for Humvees deployed in theater, contained fixed-price, cost-plus-fixed-fee, and cost-reimbursement line items, and the government challenged only the wages claimed under the cost-reimbursement (engineering services) line items, while Subcontract AMS01 (Subcontract No. 017-O2K1) was issued to Dynetics by Aviation & Missile Solutions, LLC (a joint venture between Dynetics and Camber) under an AMCOM prime contract, with all five task orders at issue issued on a firm-fixed-price level-of-effort basis. On AR005, the court rejected Dynetics' argument that the "Firm-Fixed-Price" code on the Standard Form 30 cover page made the entire contract fixed-price—that code described the undefinitized letter contract being modified—and held that the only incorporated inspection clause, FAR 52.246-2, governs "supplies," not wages for engineering services; on AMS01, the FFP-LOE structure meant payment was based on effort rather than results.

Furthermore, the Court of Federal Claims squarely rejected Dynetics' argument that general economic or commercial risks satisfy Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1). Dynetics argued that it faced risk from uncertain and broadly defined statements of work, from investing in staffing and resources without a government commitment to order more than a minimal amount of work, from incremental, IDIQ, and option-based ordering under which the government could decline to issue further work, from termination-for-convenience clauses, and from the undefinitized initial form of three contracts. The court held, quoting Fairchild, that the inquiry turns on who bears the research costs upon failure, so that none of these exposures—including the loss of a fee or profit opportunity upon termination—is the financial risk contemplated by the regulation (121 Fed. Cl. at 515–16).
Misconstruction of Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Inspection and Limitation of Cost Clauses

To overcome the absence of express contingency language in its payment schedules, Dynetics relied heavily on standard FAR clauses incorporated by reference into its government contracts. Specifically, Dynetics argued that FAR 52.246-8 ("Inspection of Research and Development—Cost-Reimbursement") in AF007 and FAR 52.246-5 ("Inspection of Services—Cost-Reimbursement") in NT001—whose inspection language resembles the provision at issue in Fairchild—placed it at the same risk as Fairchild, and that FAR 52.246-8(f)–(g) exposed it to the costs of correcting or replacing nonconforming work.

Chief Judge Campbell-Smith conducted a clause-by-clause textual analysis and held that standard FAR inspection provisions do not transform cost-reimbursement or level-of-effort contracts into risk-bearing research agreements. In examining the inspection mechanics (121 Fed. Cl. at 505), the court emphasized that although FAR 52.246-8(c) gave the government the "right to inspect and test all work called for by the contract," the AF007 contract "did not include rejection language; nor did it limit payment to work the government accepted". Moreover, under FAR 52.246-8(f), the cost of replacement or correction is determined under the Allowable Cost and Payment clause (FAR 52.216-7), with only the additional fee withheld, so that the denial of fee merely limits the contractor's profit on corrective work, and the government's right under FAR 52.246-8(g) to charge increased costs arises only if the contractor fails to proceed with reasonable promptness—a risk not attributable to the failure of the research.

Similarly, the court addressed the FAR Limitation of Cost clause (FAR 52.232-20) incorporated into NT001 when rejecting Dynetics' reliance on the Thomason Affidavit. Far from imposing financial risk on the contractor, the Limitation of Cost clause is a statutory and regulatory shield that protects a government contractor: it explicitly stipulates that the contractor is not obligated to continue performance or incur costs beyond the funded ceiling obligated by the government unless and until the Contracting Officer notifies the contractor in writing that the estimated cost ceiling has been increased. Consequently, the express terms of the FAR shielded Dynetics from involuntary cost overruns rather than exposing it to uncompensated research failure.
Evidentiary Failure: The Parol Evidence Rule, "Course of Dealing," and Lack of Contracting Officer Authority

Confronted with unambiguous contract text that guaranteed payment for incurred costs or labor hours, Dynetics attempted to introduce extrinsic evidence to prove that, in actual practice, it bore financial risk. Dynetics filed eight affidavits (Exhibits B–I), most of them from its own employees, along with affidavits from a retired MSIC contracting officer and a former MSIC Deputy Director now employed by Dynetics—including the Nicaise Affidavit (Exhibit G, addressing all sample contracts), the Hug Affidavit (Exhibit E, addressing AF007), the Williams Affidavit (Exhibit D, addressing AR005), the Bendickson Affidavit (Exhibit I, addressing BOE12), the Walker Affidavit (Exhibit H, addressing AR009), the Miller Affidavit (Exhibit C, addressing AMS01), and the Thomason (Exhibit B) and Keller (Exhibit F) Affidavits addressing NT001.

These affidavits asserted that Dynetics would rework defective or unacceptable deliverables at its own cost and absorb cost overruns out of its fee to protect its reputation and secure future work—in the Williams Affidavit's formulation, regardless of whether the product was governed by a fixed-price or cost-plus-fixed-fee CLIN. In the Thomason Affidavit regarding NT001, the retired MSIC contracting officer for the contract asserted that he expected all tasks to be completed within the amounts listed in each delivery order, that he would not modify delivery orders to allot additional funds, and that he expected Dynetics to rework unacceptable deliverables at its own cost.

The Court of Federal Claims declined to consider Dynetics' extrinsic evidence in deciding the motions and—addressing that evidence in full solely to assist the parties, without ruling on its admissibility—found it insufficient in any event, establishing three critical evidentiary doctrines for R&D tax credit litigation (121 Fed. Cl. at 512). First, the court enforced the threshold requirement of contractual ambiguity. Under federal contract law (Metric Constructors, Inc.), a court may look beyond the written text only when a contract term is ambiguous, meaning it is susceptible to more than one interpretation falling within a "zone of reasonableness". Dynetics argued that because the taxpayer and the Department of Justice disagreed during summary judgment briefing over the parties' rights and obligations under the contracts, the contracts were ipso facto ambiguous. The court rejected this circular reasoning, holding that mere litigation disagreement between a taxpayer and the IRS does not render an unambiguous contract ambiguous. The court added that Dynetics' other asserted ambiguities—undefined FAR terms, multiple or missing inspection clauses, and frequent contract modifications—would at most be patent ambiguities, which are read against the contractor because of its duty to inquire.

Second, the court held that extrinsic "course of dealing" evidence is inadmissible to vary express contract terms. Citing Alves v. United States and Barron Bancshares, Inc. v. United States, the court held that the parol evidence rule bars course-of-dealing evidence offered to modify, supplement, or interpret an unambiguous integrated agreement, and, citing Sperry Flight Systems Division of Sperry Rand Corp. v. United States, explained that a course of dealing requires conduct reflecting the parties' joint or common understanding—whereas Dynetics' affidavits described only its own unilateral contract management practices or its belief about what its customers understood. The court also rejected Dynetics' argument that the Treasury regulation's reference to "all agreements" required consideration of the course of dealing, noting that the FAR defines an "agreement" as a written instrument of understanding. Because the contracts unambiguously required the government to pay for costs incurred or hours worked, Dynetics' voluntary business practice of absorbing rework costs to preserve client goodwill and protect its corporate reputation could not alter the legal nature of the agreements.

Third, the court underscored the limits of contracting officer authority. With respect to the Thomason Affidavit on Contract NT001, the court noted that Dynetics' argument rested on the premise that Mr. Thomason, as contracting officer, had the authority to disregard the plain language of the FAR Limitation of Cost clause and compel Dynetics to perform unfunded work. The NT001 contract incorporated a Changes clause (FAR 52.243-2, Alternate II) permitting the contracting officer to make only six enumerated categories of changes, and only by written order, and nothing in it authorized converting the cost-plus-fixed-fee contract into a fixed-price contract by written order or oral understanding. The court further found that the Keller Affidavit showed no personal knowledge of the NT001 contract and that nothing in the record suggested Mr. Thomason, a former MSIC employee, had authority to present MSIC's position on its management of the contract.
Failure to Retain "Substantial Rights" Under Security Classifications, IP Clauses, and the Incidental Benefits Exclusion

In addition to failing the financial risk prong, Dynetics failed the second prong of the funded research analysis—the "substantial rights" test of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2)—on the two contracts evaluated by the court under that standard, UAH01 and Task Order 169 of NT001. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2), if a researcher retains no substantial rights in the research under the governing agreement, the research is deemed fully funded regardless of whether the researcher incurred financial risk or spent more than the contract price.

On Contract NT001, for which the government asked the court to consider only Task Order 169—preparing engineering drawings and a technical report characterizing sections of a classified foreign air-defense missile system known as "Vorlon"—the DD Form 254 security classification specification (Attachment 2 to the contract) classified the work as Top Secret with access to Sensitive Compartmented Information and restricted the reproduction, release, and use of intelligence material absent written authorization. Seeking to bring itself within the ambit of Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), Dynetics argued that the skills and advancements developed on Task Order 169 could be reused in subsequent work, that it could use the results for other intelligence agencies following MSIC authorization, that its models and analyses were severable from the intelligence material, and that FAR 52.227-11 preserved its rights in the research.

Chief Judge Campbell-Smith exposed the fatal flaw in this argument (121 Fed. Cl. at 521), writing: "Dynetics does not address the obvious question of how it could have substantial rights in the results of the research, if it needed the government's 'authorization' to use those results". The court carefully distinguished Lockheed Martin. In Lockheed Martin, the export control laws and top secret security classifications relied upon by the trial court were outside the research agreements and therefore irrelevant to the substantial rights determination, which had to be made by reference to the contracts alone. In Dynetics, by contrast, the DD Form 254 security requirements were part of the NT001 contract itself, and FAR 52.227-11 did not help Dynetics because it covers only patentable "subject inventions," while Dynetics made no argument that its engineering drawings and technical report were patentable.

Similarly, on Subcontract UAH01, paragraph 24 vested in the University all rights, title, and interest in inventions or other intellectual property rights conceived or reduced to practice in performing the work, and the court held that even if Dynetics' equation-solving and deep-space simulation work was non-patentable, other intellectual property rights such as copyright in computer code vested in the University, making it unnecessary to reach the government's alternative work-for-hire argument. Finally, to the extent Dynetics argued that performing Task Order 169 generated reusable skills and advancements, the court enforced the express bar of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2): "Incidental benefits to the taxpayer from performance of the research (for example, increased experience in a field of research) do not constitute substantial rights in the research".

body.text: Second- and Third-Order Jurisprudence: How Dynetics Reshaped the R&D Tax Credit Landscape

The analytical framework forged in Dynetics triggered a profound doctrinal shift across United States federal courts, establishing a high evidentiary barrier that continues to govern R&D tax credit litigation in the United States Tax Court and the federal circuits. Prior to 2015, taxpayers and advisory firms frequently relied on an expansive reading of Fairchild and Lockheed Martin to claim QREs on virtually any fixed-price, milestone-billed, or engineering services contract. Dynetics—decided alongside the Eleventh Circuit's opinion in Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015)—terminated that permissive approach by cementing three doctrines that subsequent courts have systematically enforced.

First, in Tangel v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2020-155, aff'd, No. 21-1405 (2d Cir. 2022), the U.S. Tax Court disallowed R&D credits for an engineering contractor whose terms and conditions designated designs as "works made for hire" and prohibited reuse without the customer's consent, applying the same contract-based substantial rights analysis articulated in Dynetics (121 Fed. Cl. at 521). Tangel confirmed that standard commercial confidentiality and IP-assignment clauses cannot be dismissed as benign non-disclosure agreements if their plain text requires client authorization to reuse research results.

Second, in United States v. Grigsby, 86 F.4th 602 (5th Cir. 2023), and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. (MBJ) v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), the Fifth and Eighth Circuits, applying the same Fairchild-based framework reflected in Dynetics (121 Fed. Cl. at 505, 515–16), dismantled the proposition that fixed-price contracts are per se unfunded. Both appellate courts held that taxpayers cannot conflate contracts for general design services or products with contracts where payment is explicitly contingent on the technical success of research, nor can taxpayers rely on inspection clauses that lack explicit rejection and refund remedies.

Third, in Smith, et al. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50 (decided June 16, 2026), the U.S. Tax Court applied the funded research precedent, including MBJ, Grigsby, Tangel, and Lockheed Martin, to an architectural and engineering partnership in a mixed decision, holding that the partnership retained substantial rights but that its research was partially funded, so that credits were available only to the extent research expenses exceeded client payments. Crucially, the taxpayers in Smith mounted a direct administrative-law challenge to the validity of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) under the U.S. Supreme Court's landmark decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 144 S. Ct. 2244 (2024), arguing that after the overruling of Chevron deference, the regulatory "substantial rights" and "contingent on success" rules exceeded the plain dictionary meaning of "funded" in I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H). The Tax Court rejected the Loper Bright challenge, affirming the continued statutory validity and binding authority of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d). Consequently, the strict two-prong contractual scrutiny articulated in Dynetics stands today as durable, post-Loper Bright federal law.
Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory, regulatory, and contract-law requirement examined in Dynetics, Inc. v. United States against the specific legal or evidentiary failures of the taxpayer and the governing standard of proof enforced by the Court of Federal Claims.

headers: Taxpayer's Specific Legal & Evidentiary Failure in Dynetics

cells: Burden of Proof & Presumption of Correctness

I.R.C. § 41(a); RCFC 56(a); Bubble Room, Inc. v. United States, 159 F.3d 553 (Fed. Cir. 1998); Estate of Rubinstein v. United States, 119 Fed. Cl. 658 (2015); Cook v. United States, 46 Fed. Cl. 110 (2000); Helvering v. Taylor, 293 U.S. 507 (1935).
Relied on assertions about how the parties informally operated under the contracts, rather than contract text, to meet its burden.

The Commissioner's determination is presumed correct, and the taxpayer bears the burden of proving by a preponderance of the evidence that the determination is incorrect and of establishing entitlement to the specific refund amount claimed.
Payment Contingency on Technical Success of Research (Financial Risk Prong)
I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(9); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2); Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995).

Claimed QREs on CPFF (AF007, NT001, the cost-reimbursement line items of AR005), CPFF level-of-effort (UAH01), T&M (BOE12), and FFP-LOE (AR009, AMS01) contracts where payment was guaranteed for allowable costs incurred or effort delivered regardless of technical outcome.

The contract must condition the contractor's right to payment on the successful result of the research—as in Fairchild, where the contractor expressly accepted total system responsibility, the government could reject nonconforming work, and payment was limited to work delivered and accepted.
Distinction Between Research Risk and General Economic Risk
Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1); Dynetics, 121 Fed. Cl. at 515–16; Fairchild, 71 F.3d at 873.

Argued that uncertain statements of work, investment in staffing without a commitment for future work, incremental and IDIQ ordering, termination-for-convenience clauses, and undefinitized contracts constituted financial risk under Section 41.

General economic risks—such as investing resources without a guaranteed commitment for future work or risking loss of profit opportunity—do not satisfy Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1); the financial risk must stem directly from the potential failure of the research itself.
Contractual Inspection, Rejection, and Acceptance Mechanics
FAR 52.246-8 (Cost-Reimbursement R&D Inspection); FAR 52.246-5 (Cost-Reimbursement Services Inspection); DAR 7-302.4 and 7-302.2; Dynetics, 121 Fed. Cl. at 505; Fairchild, 71 F.3d at 870–73.

Relied on boilerplate FAR inspection clauses in AF007 and NT001 to argue that the government could inspect and reject work, despite the absence of rejection language or payment limited to accepted work.

A right to inspect and test deliverables is insufficient alone; as in Fairchild, the contract must include rejection language and limit payment to work delivered and accepted, and correction costs that remain reimbursable (with only the fee withheld) do not shift research risk.
Cost Ceilings and Limitation of Cost Clauses
FAR 52.232-20 (Limitation of Cost); FAR 52.243-2, Alternate II (Changes); Dynetics, 121 Fed. Cl. at 512–15.

Relied on the Thomason Affidavit to argue that, on NT001, the contracting officer required completion of tasks within allotted funds and rework at Dynetics' own cost despite the cost-reimbursement terms.

Under the Limitation of Cost clause, the contractor is not obligated to continue performance beyond the estimated cost absent written notice from the Contracting Officer; an informal understanding cannot override that express term.
Contract Interpretation, Ambiguity, and the Parol Evidence Rule
Metric Constructors, Inc. v. NASA; Alves v. United States; Barron Bancshares, Inc. v. United States; Sperry Flight Systems Div. v. United States; Dynetics, 121 Fed. Cl. at 512.
Submitted eight extrinsic witness affidavits (e.g., Nicaise, Hug, Williams, Thomason) asserting an unwritten "course of dealing" where Dynetics voluntarily reworked defects at its own expense.

Written contracts govern over informal business practices; extrinsic course-of-dealing evidence is inadmissible to vary unambiguous contract terms, litigation disagreement does not create contractual ambiguity, patent ambiguities are read against the contractor, and a course of dealing requires a joint understanding rather than a unilateral practice.
Authority of Government Contracting Officials
FAR 52.243-2, Alternate II (Changes—Cost-Reimbursement); Dynetics, 121 Fed. Cl. at 512–14.

Relied on the Thomason Affidavit (NT001), from the former contracting officer, to argue that he effectively managed the CPFF contract as a fixed-price contract and compelled completion of work within allotted funds.

A contracting officer's authority is limited to the changes the contract authorizes, made by written order; nothing permits converting a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract into a fixed-price contract by written order or oral understanding.
Retention of Substantial Rights in Research Results
I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2); Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000); Dynetics, 121 Fed. Cl. at 521.

Claimed substantial rights in UAH01 and Task Order 169 of NT001 despite a subcontract clause vesting all intellectual property rights in the University and DD Form 254 security requirements requiring government authorization to use the research results.

The determination of substantial rights is governed strictly by the research agreement; if the contract vests IP ownership in the client or requires the researcher to obtain client authorization or pay to use the research results, the researcher retains no substantial rights.
Exclusion of Incidental Benefits and General Know-How
Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(a)(3); Dynetics, 121 Fed. Cl. at 519–22.

Argued that skills and advancements developed under Task Order 169 of NT001, such as improved engineering-drawing and radio-frequency identification methods, could be reused and satisfied the substantial rights test.

Increased experience, general technical know-how, and skill acquired in a field of research are merely "incidental benefits" that are expressly excluded by regulation from constituting substantial rights in the research.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial mandates of Dynetics, Inc. v. United States (and its progeny in Tangel, Grigsby, MBJ, and Smith) into actionable legal and technical practice, this section constructs two detailed industry case studies. Each scenario replicates the exact contractual, governance, and evidentiary pitfalls that proved fatal to Dynetics and demonstrates step-by-step how a United States taxpayer can restructure its project governance, technical documentation, contract clauses, and accounting systems prior to contract execution to establish an audit-ready R&D tax credit claim under I.R.C. § 41.
Case Study 1: Defense & Aerospace Systems Engineering Contractor (Overcoming the AF007, AR005, NT001, and AR009 Pitfalls)
Baseline Project Scenario and Inherent Dynetics Pitfalls

AeroVanguard Defense Systems, Inc. ("AeroVanguard"), a domestic C-corporation headquartered in Huntsville, Alabama, specializes in tactical missile guidance, hypersonic aerothermodynamics, and threat-simulation engineering. The U.S. Army Aviation & Missile Command (AMCOM) awards AeroVanguard a $14.5 million multi-CLIN contract ("Contract AV-104") to design, model, build, and wind-tunnel test an autonomous Dual-Mode Seeker and Aerodynamic Tailkit Assembly ("DMS-ATA") capable of maneuvering munitions at Mach 4.5 under high-G thermal stress.

As initially drafted by the procurement teams, Contract AV-104 contains four fatal defects identical to those in Dynetics. First, CLIN 0001 ($6.0M — Threat Modeling & Aerodynamic Simulation) is structured as a Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee (CPFF) line item incorporating FAR 52.246-8 ("Inspection of Research and Development—Cost-Reimbursement") and FAR 52.232-20 ("Limitation of Cost"), mirroring the inspection clause of Contract AF007 and the Limitation of Cost clause of Contract NT001. Second, CLIN 0002 ($4.5M — Seeker Algorithm & Software Integration) is structured as a Fixed-Price Level-of-Effort (FP-LOE) line item requiring AeroVanguard to deliver 22,500 engineering labor hours over 18 months, mirroring Contract AR009. Third, CLIN 0003 ($4.0M — Prototype Fabrication & Wind-Tunnel Testing) is structured as a Firm-Fixed-Price (FFP) line item—the type of line item the government did not challenge in Contract AR005—but incorporates only a generic inspection clause without explicit technical rejection metrics or progress-payment refund provisions. Moreover, AeroVanguard tracks all engineering labor across CLINs 0001, 0002, and 0003 under a single master job-cost code, planning to rely on program manager affidavits at audit to claim that AeroVanguard always absorbs rework costs voluntarily. Fourth, because the threat-simulation parameters involve classified intelligence data, the contract includes a DD Form 254 security classification specification and a special clause stating that "all technical data, models, software, and inventions generated under this Contract are the exclusive property of the U.S. Government, and Contractor shall not utilize or disclose any research results in any other program without the prior written authorization of the Contracting Officer"—mirroring the exact disqualifications in NT001 and UAH01 (121 Fed. Cl. at 521).

Under Dynetics, if AeroVanguard claims I.R.C. § 41 QREs under this baseline structure, 100 percent of the claim will be disallowed on summary judgment: CLIN 0001 is funded because costs are reimbursed regardless of technical success; CLIN 0002 is funded because payment is contingent on labor hours rather than research success; CLIN 0003 lacks Fairchild rejection and refund specificity; the single cost code contaminates all CLINs; program manager affidavits will be excluded under the parol evidence rule; and the prior-authorization IP clause destroys substantial rights across the entire contract.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Procurement Authority

To rescue the R&D tax credit eligibility of its development expenditures, AeroVanguard's tax counsel, government contracts legal team, and chief engineer must execute a comprehensive restructuring during solicitation negotiation—or via formal bilateral contract modification on Standard Form 30 (SF-30) signed by a warranted Contracting Officer—prior to incurring the research expenses. First, AeroVanguard negotiates with the AMCOM Contracting Officer to partition Contract AV-104 into distinct, legally severable CLINs that isolate routine or government-funded intelligence gathering from high-risk experimental hardware and algorithm development. CLIN 0001 (classified foreign threat data ingestion, where the government mandates CPFF pricing and retains exclusive classified control) is isolated as a non-creditable, funded support CLIN ($2.5M), while the core experimental design, seeker algorithm development, and aerodynamic tailkit prototyping ($12.0M) are consolidated into CLIN 0002 (Seeker Hardware/Software R&D) and CLIN 0003 (Aerodynamic Tailkit R&D) as pure, completion-based Firm-Fixed-Price (FFP) deliverables, eliminating the FP-LOE labor-hour structure of AR009 entirely.

To avoid the NT001 Thomason Affidavit failure—where Dynetics relied on a contracting officer's informal, unwritten management of a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract as if it were a fixed-price contract, beyond the authority conferred by the contract's Changes clause—AeroVanguard establishes an internal corporate governance rule prohibiting any engineering team from performing out-of-scope rework, altering technical specifications, or relying on agency representations unless memorialized in a bilateral SF-30 Contract Modification executed by the warranted Contracting Officer pursuant to FAR 43.103. Furthermore, project governance for CLINs 0002 and 0003 is tied to four formal Technical Performance Milestones: Preliminary Design Review (PDR), Critical Design Review (CDR), Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) Qualification, and Supersonic Wind-Tunnel Acceptance Testing. Governance rules prohibit the billing or final retention of milestone payments until the Contracting Officer signs a formal DD Form 250 (Material Inspection and Receiving Report) verifying that the prototype has satisfied every quantitative threshold in the Performance Work Statement (PWS).
Step 2: Re-Engineering Contract Terms (Risk & Substantial Rights Clauses)

To satisfy both prongs of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) within the "four corners" of the contract and eliminate any reliance on extrinsic "course of dealing" affidavits, AeroVanguard incorporates express provisions into Section H (Special Contract Requirements), Section E (Inspection and Acceptance), and Section I (Contract Clauses) of Contract AV-104. For FFP CLINs 0002 and 0003, FAR 52.246-8 is deleted and replaced with FAR 52.246-2 ("Inspection of Supplies—Fixed-Price") and FAR 52.232-16 ("Progress Payments"), supplemented by a tailored Special Clause H.1 (Technical Acceptance, Rejection, and Financial Risk Allocation) that establishes Fairchild-compliant rejection, uncompensated cure, and refund mechanics:

"Clause H.1: Contingency of Payment on Technical Success. Notwithstanding any other provision of this Contract, all payments (including performance-based or progress payments) under CLIN 0002 and CLIN 0003 are strictly contingent upon Contractor's successful completion of the research and development and the Government's formal technical acceptance of the deliverables on DD Form 250 in accordance with the quantitative performance parameters set forth in Attachment 1 (Technical Specifications). If any deliverable under CLIN 0002 or CLIN 0003 fails to achieve a Mach 4.5 thermal survivability threshold of >1,400°C and a Circular Error Probable (CEP) guidance accuracy of <1.5 meters during acceptance testing, the Government shall reject the deliverable. Upon rejection, Contractor shall (a) correct, redesign, and re-test the rejected deliverable entirely at Contractor's sole, uncompensated expense with zero adjustment to the contract price, or (b) if Contractor is unable to achieve technical compliance within ninety (90) days, forfeit all unpaid milestone amounts and refund to the Government within thirty (30) days all progress or milestone payments previously advanced under the rejected CLIN."

To overcome the NT001 and UAH01 substantial rights failure (121 Fed. Cl. at 521), AeroVanguard removes the blanket government ownership and "prior written authorization" restriction for CLINs 0002 and 0003. In its place, AeroVanguard incorporates FAR 52.227-11 ("Patent Rights—Ownership by the Contractor") and DFARS 252.227-7013 ("Rights in Technical Data—Other Than Commercial Products and Commercial Services"), paired with Special Clause H.2 (Allocation of Intellectual Property and Commercialization Rights):

"Clause H.2: Retention of Substantial Rights by Contractor. Pursuant to FAR 52.227-11 and DFARS 252.227-7013, Contractor shall retain full title to all Subject Inventions, foreground aerodynamic algorithms, thermal-structural designs, and un-classified technical data developed under CLIN 0002 and CLIN 0003, subject to a non-exclusive, nontransferable, irrevocable, paid-up license to the U.S. Government for government purposes. Contractor retains the unconditional, royalty-free right to use, reproduce, modify, manufacture, and commercially exploit all research results, designs, and technologies developed under CLIN 0002 and CLIN 0003 in Contractor's trade or business for any other government or commercial customer without seeking prior authorization from, or making any payment to, the Government. Classified threat parameters provided by the Government under CLIN 0001 shall remain segregated in Attachment 2 (Government Furnished Information) so that security restrictions on Government Furnished Information do not restrict Contractor's independent use of the foreground engineering results developed under CLIN 0002 and CLIN 0003."
Step 3: Restructuring Technical Documentation to Satisfy I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)

To link the contractual risk provisions directly to the statutory Four-Part Test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1), AeroVanguard implements a contemporaneous engineering documentation protocol tied to Attachment 1, the 450-page Technical Specification document. Under the business component test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(B), AeroVanguard formally defines two discrete business components corresponding strictly to the at-risk FFP line items: the DMS-ATA Seeker Signal-Processing Unit (CLIN 0002) and the Mach 4.5 Carbon-Silicon-Carbide (C/SiC) Actuated Tailfin Assembly (CLIN 0003).

To substantiate technological uncertainty under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(B), the Lead Systems Engineer authors a dated Technical Uncertainty & Baseline Capability Dossier at project inception demonstrating that while standard munitions tailkits operate up to Mach 1.8, existing engineering capability cannot establish the optimal structural geometry, actuator torque-to-weight ratio, or thermal-expansion tolerances required to prevent control-surface flutter and sensor delamination at Mach 4.5 shockwave boundary layers. Furthermore, to substantiate a structured process of experimentation under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C), engineers record every design iteration in AeroVanguard's Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) database, capturing the specific scientific hypothesis tested (such as varying leading-edge sweep angles between 32° and 41° in computational fluid dynamics [CFD] models), the simulation or wind-tunnel test results, specific failures against the Clause H.1 acceptance criteria (such as Prototype Iteration 2 suffering actuator thermal seizure at 1,180°C during HIL testing, failing the 1,400°C contractual threshold), and the resulting engineering redesign.
Step 4: Restructuring Experimentation Tracking and Financial Accounting

In AeroVanguard's Deltek Costpoint ERP system, the accounting department establishes a rigid cost-accounting boundary between funded and unfunded CLINs. WBS 104.01 (CLIN 0001 - CPFF Threat Analysis) is flagged in the tax engine as 100% Excluded Funded Research. Conversely, WBS 104.02 (CLIN 0002 - FFP Seeker R&D) and WBS 104.03 (CLIN 0003 - FFP Tailkit R&D) are mapped to dedicated sub-accounts tracking direct engineering labor (by employee, date, and specific technical task), prototype fabrication supplies under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), and cloud high-performance CFD computing time under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii).

When Prototype Iteration 2 fails the preliminary wind-tunnel test against Clause H.1 specifications, all engineering labor and material costs incurred to diagnose the failure, redesign the thermal barrier, and manufacture Prototype Iteration 3 are logged to WBS 104.03.RW (Uncompensated Contractual Cure). Rather than relying on a post-hoc witness affidavit claiming a "course of dealing," AeroVanguard produces contemporaneous general ledger entries, rejected DD Form 250 test reports, and subsequent accepted DD Form 250 sign-offs proving that payment was legally and factually contingent on successful research.
Case Study 2: Commercial & Joint Venture Advanced Hardware Subcontractor (Overcoming the BOE12, AMS01, and Tangel/MBJ Pitfalls)
Baseline Project Scenario and Inherent Dynetics Pitfalls

NexGen Thermal & Power Systems, LLC ("NexGen"), an engineering and manufacturing firm taxed as a partnership (or C-corporation joint venture analogous to AMS01), designs solid-state power distribution and micro-channel liquid cooling architectures for commercial electric aviation and satellite payloads. NexGen enters into a master subcontract ("Subcontract NG-88") with Apex Aerospace Corp. ("Apex"), a Tier-1 commercial aerospace prime contractor, to develop a high-density, 1.2-megawatt Silicon-Carbide (SiC) Cryogenic Inverter Module ("CIM-1200") for a next-generation regional hybrid-electric aircraft.

Subcontract NG-88 contains four structural flaws that directly replicate the disqualifications in BOE12, AMS01, Tangel, and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson (MBJ). First, mirroring Contract BOE12 in Dynetics and the capped contracts in Geosyntec, Subcontract NG-88 is structured as a Time-and-Materials (T&M) agreement with a "Not-to-Exceed" (NTE) cap of $5.2 million. NexGen submits monthly invoices billing Apex at fixed hourly rates ($185/hour for Senior Electrical Engineers; $145/hour for Thermal Analysts) plus material costs, payable Net 30 upon invoice submission. Second, like the contracts in MBJ (100 F.4th 986) and the level-of-effort task orders in AMS01, the Statement of Work states only that NexGen will "provide engineering assistance, thermal modeling, and prototype design services to support Apex's propulsion program," without tying payments to specific technical performance barometers or giving Apex a contractual right to demand a refund of invoiced payments if the inverter fails to reach 1.2-megawatt efficiency targets. Third, NexGen's Managing Partner plans to testify that if the engineering team hits the $5.2 million NTE cap before the inverter works, NexGen will continue working free of charge to protect its relationship with Apex—the exact "course of dealing" argument rejected in Dynetics (121 Fed. Cl. at 512). Fourth, Paragraph 14 of Apex's standard commercial Purchase Order Terms and Conditions states: "All deliverables, circuit topologies, schematics, firmware, and technical data prepared by Seller in connection with this Order shall be 'works made for hire' and the sole property of Buyer. Seller shall keep all such design information strictly confidential and shall not reuse any design, technology, or research outcome created hereunder for any third party without Buyer's prior written consent"—mirroring UAH01, NT001, and the fatal clause in Tangel v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2020-155.

Under Dynetics and Tangel, NexGen's R&D credit claim is completely unsustainable: T&M monthly invoicing is not contingent on research success; the NTE cap combined with informal willingness to absorb overruns does not create Fairchild risk; and Paragraph 14 strips NexGen of all substantial rights, rendering the research 100 percent funded under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2).
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Eliminating Extrinsic "Handshake" Practices

To transform Subcontract NG-88 into an unqualified, credit-eligible research arrangement under I.R.C. § 41, NexGen's legal and technical leadership must overhaul the governance framework before commencing engineering work. Because the Court of Federal Claims in Dynetics held that courts will not look to informal practices, emails, or "course of dealing" affidavits when a contract is unambiguous (121 Fed. Cl. at 512), NexGen's corporate governance policy mandates that all risk-allocation and IP terms be expressly written into a Master Research & Development Addendum ("R&D Addendum") that explicitly supersedes Apex's standard Purchase Order boilerplate via an Order of Precedence Clause.

Simultaneously, governance of the CIM-1200 development is removed from routine monthly accounts-payable invoicing and placed under a formal Joint Technical Acceptance Board (JTAB) comprising Apex's Chief Propulsion Engineer and NexGen's VP of Engineering. Under the JTAB charter, no invoice may be approved or settled on a time-worked basis; every payment event requires a formal Certificate of Technical Milestone Compliance verifying that the physical or simulated deliverable achieved the contractual performance metrics.
Step 2: Re-Engineering Contract Terms (Converting T&M to Milestone-Contingent FFP & Retaining Substantial Rights)

NexGen and Apex execute the binding R&D Addendum amending Subcontract NG-88 across three critical dimensions. First, the T&M hourly rate schedule and NTE cap are deleted in their entirety. Subcontract NG-88 is converted into a $5.2 Million Firm-Fixed-Price Completion Contract payable strictly across three outcome-based technical milestones, governed by Section 4 (Contingency of Payment, Technical Rejection, and Refund Remedy):

"Section 4.1: Payment Contingent on Technical Success of Research. Buyer and Seller agree that Buyer is contracting solely for the successful technical result of Seller's research—specifically, a flight-weight CIM-1200 Cryogenic Inverter Module meeting all quantitative specifications in Exhibit A (99.1% power conversion efficiency at 1.2 MW continuous load, total harmonic distortion <1.2%, and specific power density ≥18 kW/kg)—and not for engineering labor hours or design services.

Section 4.2: Milestone Acceptance, Rejection, and Clawback. Fixed-price payments for Milestone 1 ($1.2M — Validated Electromagnetic & Thermal Architecture), Milestone 2 ($2.0M — Full-Scale Breadboard Load Test at 1.2 MW), and Milestone 3 ($2.0M — Environmental, EMI, and Thermal-Vacuum Qualification Unit) shall become earned and payable only upon Buyer's written technical verification that the deliverable satisfies Exhibit A specifications. If any milestone deliverable fails to meet Exhibit A specifications, Buyer shall issue a Formal Notice of Technical Rejection. Upon rejection, Seller shall redesign, re-fabricate, and re-test the deliverable entirely at Seller's sole financial expense. If Seller fails to cure the technical non-conformity and achieve Exhibit A performance standards within one hundred twenty (120) days of rejection, Buyer may terminate this Subcontract for technical failure, whereupon Seller shall forfeit all unpaid contract balances and refund to Buyer within fifteen (15) business days 100% of all prior milestone payments received under this Subcontract."

Second, to eliminate the Dynetics (121 Fed. Cl. at 521) and Tangel disqualification under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2), Paragraph 14 of the Purchase Order is deleted and replaced by Section 7 (Intellectual Property Ownership and Substantial Rights Allocation):

"Section 7.1: Ownership and Unconditional Right to Use Research Results. Seller shall retain sole ownership of all Pre-Existing Background IP and shall retain joint ownership (or, alternatively, an irrevocable, perpetual, worldwide, non-exclusive, royalty-free, fully paid-up commercial license) in and to all Foreground Inventions, micro-channel cooling geometries, SiC gate-driver topologies, firmware algorithms, and research results conceived or developed in the performance of this Subcontract. Seller is expressly authorized to use, manufacture, market, license, and commercially exploit all such Foreground Inventions and research results in Seller's trade or business for any other customer or product line without obtaining Buyer's prior consent and without paying any royalty, fee, or consideration to Buyer.

Section 7.2: Narrowed Scope of Confidentiality. Confidentiality obligations under this Subcontract shall apply strictly and exclusively to Buyer's proprietary airframe interface dimensions provided in Exhibit B (Buyer Furnished Data) and shall in no way restrict Seller's independent right to use or commercialize the research results, inverter architectures, or thermal designs developed by Seller hereunder."

Third, preserving substantial rights under Section 7 provides essential fallback protection against "partially funded" disallowance under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3). Even if an IRS examiner were to challenge a specific ancillary task order as lacking full payment contingency, preserving substantial rights ensures that the research is never treated as fully funded under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2); instead, under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3), any cost overruns incurred by NexGen above the funded payment amount remain eligible for the pro-rata research credit.
Step 3: Restructuring Technical Documentation

To establish the degree of technical specificity required by Fairchild and MBJ, NexGen attaches a 120-page Exhibit A (Technical Performance & Qualification Specification) to Subcontract NG-88 establishing objective, pass/fail engineering metrics, including partial-discharge voltage thresholds at 35,000 feet simulated altitude, junction temperature limits of <115°C under transient 1.5 MW surge loads, and stray inductance <8 nanohenries.

Concurrently, NexGen's engineering team maintains a structured GitLab and Ansys simulation repository documenting the iterative process of experimentation under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C). The repository records the baseline technical uncertainty that conventional busbar and cold-plate designs exhibit excessive parasitic inductance (>22 nH) and localized boiling instability when switching 1,200 Volts at 50 kilohertz under cryogenic/sub-zero operating conditions. It then documents the systematic modeling and bench-testing of four distinct laminated busbar dielectric geometries and three micro-channel pin-fin configurations, archiving high-voltage oscilloscope traces, thermal-imaging logs, and dielectric breakdown reports alongside each prototype serial number to link every engineering hour directly to resolving the technical uncertainties required to pass Milestone 1, 2, and 3 acceptance tests.
Step 4: Restructuring Experimentation Tracking and Financial Risk Verification

NexGen reconfigures its enterprise accounting and invoicing software so that external customer invoices sent to Apex reference only the fixed-price deliverable milestones (Milestones 1, 2, and 3) accompanied by the signed Certificate of Technical Milestone Compliance, eliminating all hourly billing artifacts. Internally, NexGen's engineers record daily timecards mapped to specific experimental hypotheses, such as Code NG88-EXP-02: Laminated Busbar Parasitic Inductance Mitigation Testing. In the general ledger, all project expenditures ($4.85M in QRE wages, prototype SiC wafer supplies, and environmental chamber testing costs) are carried on the balance sheet and work-in-process ledger as Unbilled At-Risk R&D Costs Subject to Contractual Rejection until each technical milestone is formally accepted by the JTAB and the contractual clawback risk under Section 4.2 is satisfied.

cells: Contract Pricing & Payment Mechanism
CPFF (AF007, NT001, UAH01), T&M (BOE12), and FP-LOE (AR009, AMS01) structures paying for costs incurred or effort delivered.
Outcome-based Firm-Fixed-Price (FFP) CLINs/milestones where payment is earned solely upon delivery and acceptance of a technically compliant product.
Inspection, Rejection & Remedy Clauses
Standard FAR 52.246-8 and 52.246-5 inspection clauses lacking rejection language, with correction costs remaining reimbursable.
Express Fairchild-compliant clauses mandating rejection for technical non-compliance, 100% uncompensated contractor cure, and refund of prior advances upon failure.
Evidentiary Basis for Risk Allocation
Post-hoc witness affidavits claiming an informal "course of dealing" to absorb overruns and rework.
Express written risk-allocation clauses within the four corners of the contract or bilateral SF-30 modifications signed by a warranted Contracting Officer.
Intellectual Property & Substantial Rights
Clauses vesting all IP in the customer (UAH01) or security requirements conditioning use of results on customer authorization (NT001).
Explicit retention of contractor title (FAR 52.227-11) or an unconditional, royalty-free commercial license to exploit foreground research results without customer permission.
Project Accounting & Cost Segregation
Treating a contract with mixed fixed-price and cost-reimbursement line items as wholly fixed-price (AR005) or relying on general skills and experience as substantial rights (NT001).
Granular WBS sub-accounts isolating funded CPFF support CLINs from at-risk FFP R&D CLINs and separately tracking uncompensated cure/rework expenses.

body.text: Strategic Synthesis for United States Tax Practitioners

The Court of Federal Claims' ruling in Dynetics, Inc. and Subsidiaries v. United States, 121 Fed. Cl. 492 (2015), remains the definitive judicial warning that R&D tax credit qualification under I.R.C. § 41 cannot be engineered retroactively during an IRS audit or refund litigation through employee affidavits or appeals to industry custom. Because federal courts strictly apply the parol evidence rule and evaluate both financial risk (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1)) and substantial rights (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2)) exclusively by reference to the unambiguous text of the governing agreements, tax counsel must intervene upstream during contract formation. By segregating cost-reimbursement tasks from milestone-contingent fixed-price deliverables, embedding explicit technical rejection and refund remedies, and carving out unconditional rights to exploit foreground research results without client authorization, taxpayers can insulate their R&D tax credit claims from disallowance under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H).
